title: One entry
why: A pipeline starts at one place, so a run is always the same run and every stage is reached from it.
source: Hohpe and Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns (2003), Pipes and Filters

title: Each stage declares its input and output
why: A stage that names what it takes and what it gives can be read, replaced and checked on its own.
source: Dagster documentation, Ops and assets: inputs and outputs are declared (docs.dagster.io)

title: Data passes only along the edges
why: A value carried beside the declared flow (a global, a shared file, the environment, a cache, a shared context) is a hidden dependency the map cannot show.
source: Hohpe and Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns (2003), Pipes and Filters: filters share no state

title: Every router is total, its branches explicit
why: A router that meets a kind it does not handle drops the work silently; every branch is named by its condition and an unknown kind has a route.
source: Hohpe and Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns (2003), Content-Based Router and Invalid Message Channel

title: A fan-out has its fan-in
why: Work split into parallel branches is gathered again in one place, so a missing branch is noticed.
source: Hohpe and Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns (2003), Splitter, Aggregator and Scatter-Gather

title: Each stage is testable and re-runnable alone
why: A stage that can be run again on the same input with the same result can be retried, resumed and tested without the whole run.
source: Apache Airflow documentation, Best Practices: tasks should be idempotent (airflow.apache.org)

title: Every failure has a route
why: A stage that fails sends its work somewhere named (skip, retry, a failure lane), never nowhere.
source: Hohpe and Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns (2003), Dead Letter Channel

title: No dead stages and no unread outputs
why: A stage nothing reaches, or an output nobody reads, is cost without value and hides what really runs.
source: Fowler, Refactoring, 2nd edition (2018), Remove Dead Code

title: Slow and risky stages are marked
why: The stages that call the network, a model, an external tool or run long are where time and failures concentrate; they carry a timeout and are visible.
source: Nygard, Release It!, 2nd edition (2018), Timeouts and Bulkheads
